# Worked Instances {#sec-instances}

The trichotomy of @sec-theorem is stated over append-only records
specifically. This section introduces its companion theorem, states it
over a more general structure, and then works the framework on real
cases — a generality demonstration, not a survey of examples chosen
after the fact.

## The verification ceiling: a companion, not a corollary

Generalize from a single append-only record to a well-founded
justification structure: a directed acyclic graph of artifacts, each
either a leaf or carrying a derived record that names its own inputs,
together with a fail-closed classification of every artifact into
exactly one of a small number of trust buckets, relative to an admitted
policy $P$ and evidence clock $\sigma$.

::: {.theorem}
**The verification ceiling.** For such a structure:

(i) **Gate** (inherited from the trichotomy): an artifact's genuineness
    or binding claim, under an explicit underdetermination hypothesis,
    admits no evidence scheme over any commitment.

(ii) **Completeness**: every artifact in the structure's closure is
    booked into exactly one bucket, and every piece of admitted evidence
    a positive verdict depends on is enumerated in that artifact's
    basis — nothing is silently trusted.

(iii) **Minimality**: the trust surface of an artifact contains the seed
    set required by *every* scheme for it — because (i) makes the
    genesis claim permanently underivable — and equality between the
    trust surface and the seed set is therefore the *ceiling*: a system
    achieving it cannot be improved upon.
:::

This is a companion theorem, not a corollary of `TT-snap`/`TT-end`. The
trichotomy's vocabulary — records, contexts, claims, commitments,
schemes — and the ceiling's vocabulary — artifacts, buckets, policies,
snapshots, a total classification function — share no object either is
directly definable in terms of. The only bridge between them is the
gate: an artifact's genuineness claim, once cast as a record claim,
*is* an instance of the trichotomy's own determination gate. Everything
else in the ceiling — its completeness and minimality machinery — is the
companion theorem's own content, proved independently.

## Two instantiations, because one instance is a special case and two is a theory

The ceiling is instantiated twice in this paper's scope, over genuinely
disjoint domains, to demonstrate that the *generality* of the companion
theorem is itself a claim being defended, not merely asserted:

**Identity.** A cryptographic identity system whose record is a hash
chain and whose genesis is a single binding commitment. This instance's
impossibility content is fully machine-checkable with no conditional
frontier — there is no forced-generator or Rice-theoretic tightness
result standing between the model and the theorem, unlike the build
domain below. It is the paper's cleanest demonstration that the
completeness and minimality machinery is not build-specific.

**Source-build integrity** *(follow-up paper, cited, not included)*. A
source-build provenance system whose genesis is a corroboration quorum
over source classes. This instance carries build-domain-specific
frontier machinery — format/parse gates, corroboration conditions,
tightness results resting on Rice and Rice–Shapiro applied to a forced
generator — that is conditional and prose-grade rather than fully
machine-checked, and is kept out of this paper's flagship scope
precisely to keep the flagship's own epistemic grade uniform. It is
cited here only to demonstrate that the companion theorem has already
been carried to a second, independent domain.

## The extended worked example: split-view, resolved without a fourth axis

A verifier facing two different views of what is claimed to be the same
append-only log — a *split-view*, or equivocation, attack — looks at
first glance like it needs a fourth axis: neither determination,
certifiability, nor monotonicity as defined in @sec-model obviously
names "my two sources disagree." It does not. The attack decomposes,
without remainder, into two things the trichotomy already owns:

1. **Per-verifier**: "my anchor commits a prefix of the canonical
   record." For a fixed anchor, this claim is determined, monotone, and
   certifiable *over the canonical record* — the verifier's actual
   difficulty is that its only access to the canonical record is the
   anchor itself. The trust spent here is the admitted anchor, an
   entailment move (@sec-cures) against $P$, not a new axis.
2. **Cross-verifier**: "the two views I've been shown are consistent
   with each other." Posed over the joint record of shown views, this
   claim is determined and certifiable — a Merkle consistency proof is
   literally its certificate — and **non-monotone**: two views
   consistent today can diverge tomorrow. This is exactly the trichotomy's
   monotonicity-failure case, `EON` applies directly, and its cure table
   (@sec-cures) predicts the deployed defenses verbatim: entailment via a
   witness quorum or gossip protocol (cosigned checkpoints), restriction
   to "consistent as of time $t$," or an accepted expiry window.

A sharper fact falls out for free: divergence, once it exists, is
*permanent* under further extension of both views — two records that
disagree at some position remain disagreeing at that position forever.
So *equivocation* is itself monotone and affirmable — its evidence, once
obtained, endures — while *honesty* is refutative: never provable
forever, only ever falsifiable at the next check. That asymmetry is why
gossip protocols work at all, and why "this log is honest" can only ever
be held as an expiring, snapshot-grade confidence rather than an
enduring one. The framework does not just classify the attack; it
explains the shape of the field's actual defense against it.

A fourth axis would have to make verification fail for a claim that is
determined, certifiable, *and* monotone; neither component of the
split-view decomposition does that. This is the strongest available
validation of the three-axis taxonomy against a real, adversarial case,
not merely a worked textbook example.
